segments.text: Brand B says its phone battery lasts longer. You test five phones of each: A averages seven hours, B averages ten.
segments.caption: Brand B says its phone battery lasts longer. You test 5 phones of each: A averages 7 hours, B averages 10.

segments.text: A real difference, or just luck? Let's settle it with a t-test.
segments.caption: A real difference, or just luck? Let's settle it with a t-test.

segments.text: Here's the textbook definition.
segments.caption: Here's the textbook definition.

segments.text: A two-sample t-test is a hypothesis test that checks whether the means of two independent groups are significantly different, when the population standard deviations are unknown.
segments.caption: A two-sample t-test is a hypothesis test that checks whether the means of two independent groups are significantly different, when the population standard deviations are unknown.

segments.text: Use it to compare the averages of two separate groups, when sigma is unknown and the samples are small.
segments.caption: Use it to compare the averages of two separate groups, when sigma is unknown and the samples are small.

segments.text: Five phones each, sigma unknown: that's us.
segments.caption: 5 phones each, sigma unknown: that's us.

scenes.title: Steps 1 and 2: one tail or two

segments.text: Step one: H zero says both brands last the same on average.
segments.caption: Step one: H0 says both brands last the same on average.

segments.text: H one is two-tailed if they could differ either way, or one-tailed if we only ask: does B last longer?
segments.caption: H1 is two-tailed if they could differ either way, or one-tailed if we only ask: does B last longer?

segments.text: Step two: alpha, five percent. Two-tailed splits it, two point five percent per tail. One-tailed puts all five percent on the right. We'll do both.
segments.caption: Step two: alpha, 5%. Two-tailed splits it, 2.5% per tail. One-tailed puts all 5% on the right. We'll do both.

segments.text: Step three: the formula. t equals the gap between the two averages, over the standard error of that gap.
segments.caption: Step three: the formula. t equals the gap between the two averages, over the standard error of that gap.

segments.text: The standard error uses the pooled variance, s-p squared, and both sample sizes.
segments.caption: The standard error uses the pooled variance, sp squared, and both sample sizes.

segments.text: First, the averages: A is seven hours, B is ten. So the gap is three.
segments.caption: First, the averages: A is 7 hours, B is 10. So the gap is 3.

segments.text: Next, each variance. For A, square each value's distance from seven: one, one, zero, four, four. They add up to ten.
segments.caption: Next, each variance. For A, square each value's distance from 7: 1, 1, 0, 4, 4. They add up to 10.

segments.text: Divide by n minus one, four: the variance is two point five. Brand B is the same: two point five.
segments.caption: Divide by n - 1, 4: the variance is 2.5. Brand B is the same: 2.5.

segments.text: Pooled variance: two point five. Standard error: the square root of two point five, times a fifth plus a fifth. That's root one, which is one.
segments.caption: Pooled variance: 2.5. Standard error: the square root of 2.5, times a fifth plus a fifth. That's root 1, which is 1.

segments.text: So t equals three over one: t equals three.
segments.caption: So t equals 3 over 1: t equals 3.

segments.text: The t table needs the degrees of freedom: five plus five, minus two, equals eight.
segments.caption: The t table needs the degrees of freedom: 5 + 5 - 2 = 8.

segments.text: Small samples are less certain, so the t curve has fatter tails, and bigger cut-offs.
segments.caption: Small samples are less certain, so the t curve has fatter tails, and bigger cut-offs.

segments.text: Two-tailed first. A t table lists critical values directly.
segments.caption: Two-tailed first. A t table lists critical values directly.

segments.text: Row eight, column two-tailed zero point zero five: the critical value is two point three zero six.
segments.caption: Row 8, column two-tailed 0.05: the critical value is 2.306.

segments.text: Beyond plus or minus two point three zero six is the critical region, with area alpha.
segments.caption: Beyond ±2.306 is the critical region, with area alpha.

segments.text: For p: our t of three sits between two point eight nine six and three point three five five, so p is between zero point zero one and zero point zero two. Software says zero point zero one seven.
segments.caption: For p: our t of 3 sits between 2.896 and 3.355, so p is between 0.01 and 0.02. Software says 0.017.

segments.text: Our t of three is in the critical region, and p is below alpha. Both methods agree: reject H zero.
segments.caption: Our t of 3 is in the critical region, and p is below alpha. Both methods agree: reject H0.

segments.text: Now one-tailed: does B last longer? t is still three.
segments.caption: Now one-tailed: does B last longer? t is still 3.

segments.text: The one-tailed column gives one point eight six zero, and p halves to zero point zero zero eight five.
segments.caption: The one-tailed column gives 1.860, and p halves to 0.0085.

segments.text: Three is beyond one point eight six zero: reject again. Brand B really lasts longer. Save this for your interview.
segments.caption: 3 is beyond 1.860: reject again. Brand B really lasts longer. Save this for your interview.
